cite: In re Bloomingdale, 73 N.Y. St. Rep. 350
notes: The case concerns a storekeeper’s liquor license and does not concern compensated residential occupancy.

cite: Kernochan v. Wilkens, 73 N.Y. St. Rep. 853
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: The decision concerns a long-term commercial lease of store property, not occupancy of a dwelling or rooms.

cite: Crampton v. Brooklyn Elevated Railroad, 73 N.Y. St. Rep. 723
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: The lessee’s practice of leasing furnished rooms is mentioned only as background to an elevated-railroad valuation dispute; the court does not decide its legality or legal character.

cite: Chautauqua Assembly v. Alling, 12 N.Y. St. Rep. 767
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: The court held that using a family residence to keep boarders and lodgers for hire did not, by itself, violate a lease authorizing use as a private residence. It nevertheless enforced a reasonable association by-law requiring special consent for that activity and affirmed the injunction against the householder.

quotes.text: The referee has found that there is a framed house upon the lot which the defendant uses as a private residence for himself and his family during the entire year, and that he also keeps boarders and lodgers therein for hire, without the consent of the plaintiff and against its will.

We think, therefore, there is nothing in the habendum clause which should be held to restrain the defendant from doing what he is shown to have done, by way of keeping boarders and lodgers for hire, at his residence.
The rules and regulations thus made and enforced were reasonable, and such as the association had the right to make.

If these views are correct, it follows that the defendant in keeping boarders and lodgers for hire is violating a by-law enacted by the lessor which was binding upon the lessees and which the plaintiff has the right to enforce against him. The result is that the judgment, so far as it grants an injunction, should be affirmed, and in all other respects, reversed.

notes: Mixed because the court rejected an implied private-residence restriction on keeping boarders but enforced the separate by-law requiring the association’s consent.

cite: Smith v. Rector of St. Philip's Church, 12 N.Y. St. Rep. 783
holding_summary: The court held that a lessor’s knowing acceptance of rent for years could be construed as a license to use the building as an apartment house, preventing forfeiture for underletting. It also stated that letting rooms to lodgers is not a breach of a covenant against underletting.

quotes.text: It was shown on the trial that the house erected by the plaintiff was an apartment house, and that the plaintiff occupied one range of rooms and let the other apartments to tenants by the month, by verbal lease, the rent being exacted each month in advance.

But passing this question, we are of opinion that the conduct of the defendant in receiving for a series of years without objection, the rent due on the lease, with knowledge of the actual situation, should, if necessary, be construed as a license to use and occupy the building as an apartment house, and not as a mere waiver from time to time of a particular antecedent breach of the covenant.

It is consistent with the circumstances and with fair dealing to construe the acts and silence of the defendant as an assent that the somewhat peculiar interest created by the letting of apartments from time to time for brief periods, was not an under-letting or parting with any interest in the demised premises, within the meaning of the covenant.
Letting rooms to lodgers is held not to be a breach of a covenant against under-letting.

notes: The plaintiff occupied part of the apartment house and let the remaining apartments by the month.

cite: Derhoof v. Agricultural Insurance of Watertown, 12 N.Y. St. Rep. 341
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: The court held that whether the partly rented dwelling remained occupied within the meaning of its fire-insurance policy should have been submitted to the jury. It further held that the insurer was bound by its agents’ knowledge of the dwelling’s unusual occupancy and could not automatically rely on the occupancy condition to defeat coverage.

quotes.text: In July, 1878, the defendant gave consent that a portion of the house might be rented, which consent was as follows: “ Consent given to rent part of said dwelling.” After that a tenant occupied a portion of the house, and the children occupied the remainder as before.

A careful examination of the facts and authorities relating to this question, inclines us to the opinion, that under the peculiar circumstances of this case, the question of the occupancy of the house, was a question which should have been submitted to the jury under proper instructions from the court.

We think the knowledge of the defendant’s agents must be regarded as its knowledge, and hence it must be presumed either that the defendant by mistake omitted to state in its policy that the house was unoccupied, or occupied only in the manner stated to them by the plaintiff, or waived the provision as to occupancy, or held itself es-topped from setting it up.

notes: The owner’s children occupied part of the dwelling while a tenant rented another portion; the precise starting date of the tenancy is not stated, but the chronology indicates an occupancy lasting months.

cite: Douglass v. Seiferd, 75 N.Y. St. Rep. 698
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: The court held that advance payments of one year’s rent and later six months’ rent defeated the tenant’s contention that the flat was let by the month and established a yearly hiring. It also held that leaving the keys with an unauthorized janitress did not effect a surrender.

quotes.text: The issue contested at the trial was whether the hiring was by the month or by the year, it being conceded that if the hiring was by the year, and there was no effectual surrender, the plaintiff would he entitled to recover the amount claimed; if, on the other hand, the letting was a monthly one, or there had been a valid surrender, the defendant should prevail.

But it is undisputed that the tenant paid one year’s rent in advance from May 1, 1892, to May 1, 1893, and in May, 1895, paid six months’ rent at one time, up to November 1, 1895, and these facts destroy the, implication of a monthly hiring.
Under these- circumstances, it seems clear to us that the hiring was by the year, that there was no valid surrender, and that the landlord was entitled to a verdict.

notes: Adverse only in the limited sense that the court rejected the claimed month-to-month characterization of a residential flat; this was not a police-power or boarding-house regulation case.

cite: Sage v. Mayor, 75 N.Y. St. Rep. 1310
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
notes: The case concerns title to reclaimed tideway and riparian rights, not residential occupancy.
The case concerns whether a building erected by a trespasser became part of the realty; landlord-tenant doctrine appears only by analogy.

cite: Williams v. Whedon, 15 N.Y. St. Rep. 265
notes: The case concerns a surviving partner’s authority to assign partnership assets for creditors.

cite: Reynolds v. Reynolds, 15 N.Y. St. Rep. 464
court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
notes: The case concerns a crop-sharing farm agreement and ownership of crops, not compensated occupancy of dwelling rooms.
